subtitle: Tuesday, 3 November 2026
editor_note: This edition looks at how AI is being measured against the practical tasks people face every day, and at the growing efforts to keep increasingly capable systems safe and accountable. We also cover notable moves in government and national-security circles, including fresh debates over how AI should be governed and even what it should be called. Together these stories highlight why thoughtful oversight and clear standards matter as the technology advances.

items.title: LifeVal
items.summary: OpenAI has introduced a new benchmark called LifeVal, which is a standardised test designed to measure how well AI tools help ordinary people complete everyday tasks. Rather than scoring AI on abstract puzzles, LifeVal focuses on practical, real-life situations such as finding childcare, managing personal finances, and navigating government paperwork. The aim is to judge whether AI is genuinely useful in the kinds of activities that fill people's daily lives, not just whether it performs well on technical exams. For public-sector organisations, this is notable because it points toward measuring AI by its usefulness to citizens, including tasks like completing official forms and accessing public services. It also signals a broader industry shift toward evaluating AI on everyday value rather than purely on raw technical ability.

items.title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
items.summary: Researchers are exploring a method called "reverse game theory," also known as mechanism design, to help keep powerful AI systems behaving as intended. The idea is to design the rules and incentives around an AI so that it is naturally rewarded for following the rules and discouraged from breaking them, rather than relying only on direct instructions. This matters because as AI models grow more capable and act more independently, safety researchers worry about so-called "rogue agents" that could act against human interests or even break laws. The approach borrows long-standing ideas from economics, where systems are structured so that participants acting in their own interest still produce good outcomes overall. For non-specialists, the key takeaway is that controlling advanced AI may depend as much on well-designed incentives as on the technology itself.

items.title: Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test
items.summary: In late September, US President Trump signed an executive order instructing government agencies to stop using the term "artificial intelligence" and instead call it "Super Intelligence." This article examines which companies and organisations are complying with the rebranding directive and how the change is being received across the technology sector. The move is largely about terminology and political messaging rather than any change in the underlying technology, but it has sparked debate about how governments shape public understanding of AI. For readers in the public sector, it is a reminder that language and framing around AI can be politically charged and vary significantly between countries. It also illustrates how national leaders are increasingly trying to assert influence over how AI is described and governed.

items.title: OpenAI appoints Dan Driscoll as Senior Counselor for National Security Modernization
items.summary: OpenAI has appointed Dan Driscoll as a Senior Counselor for National Security Modernization, a role focused on advising the company on the responsible use of AI in national-security contexts. His remit includes strengthening cyber resilience and supporting collaboration with the United States and its allies. The appointment reflects a broader trend of AI companies building closer ties with governments and defence-related institutions as the technology becomes central to national strategy. For public-sector readers, it highlights how major AI developers are positioning themselves as partners to government on sensitive matters of security and modernisation. It also underscores the growing importance of placing experienced advisors at the intersection of advanced technology and public policy.

items.title: Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI
items.summary: Anthropic, a leading AI company, has warned that it is close to achieving what is known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI — the point at which an AI system becomes capable enough to improve and train itself. If reached, this could trigger a rapid acceleration in AI capabilities, because the technology would be advancing itself rather than relying solely on human engineers. Some researchers view this milestone with serious concern, seeing it as a moment that could become difficult to control or reverse. The warning is significant because it comes from a company at the frontier of AI development, not from outside critics, lending it added weight. For a general audience, the main point is that the pace of AI progress may speed up considerably, making robust safety measures and oversight more urgent than ever.
